title: Street Talk: HSBC puts $20b in deposits up for sale amid retail banking exit
full_text:
HSBC has given advisers at Citi the all-clear to kick off an auction of about $20 billion in deposits, marking the final stage of the global giant's exit from retail banking in Australia after four decades.
A month after selling a $36 billion book of home and personal loans to private equity giant Blackstone, Citi is in "active engagement" with the four major banks, which are among the parties to have expressed interest, according to people briefed on the mooted deal who spoke on conditionof anonymity.
HSBC is hoping to sign by the fourth quarter of the financial year, and the sale is not being run as a "wide, competitive auction", they said. Rather, HSBC and Citi are working with a small group of potential buyers and are keen to establish discussions with one party within months.
The London-based lender has committed to retaining an Australian presence in corporate and private banking. Its local presence dates back to 1986, when the Hawke government opened the banking market to foreign competitors. Over the next four decades, however, it has had limited success in taking share from the major local retail banks.
The latest monthly banking data from the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority shows HSBC Australia had just 1 per cent of the household deposits market share and about 1.5 per cent each for owner-occupier and investor home loans,as of July 31.
It flagged its plans to wind up that part of the business more than a year ago. HSBC's deposit book stands at $38.8 billion, of which about $20 billion represents household savings, people briefed on the matter said.
Already the country's two largest retail banks, Commonwealth Bank and Westpac, are stealthily chasing HBSC's mortgage customers, as revealed by The Australian Financial Review last week. Both are independently contacting mortgage brokers seeking to refinance HSBC customers en masse.
The retail pullback comes amid a sweeping overhaul under George Elhedery, who was appointed HSBC chief executive in late 2024.
HSBC's local executive, Steve Hughes, has flagged that the bank will pivot towards companies with more than $500 million in annual turnover that are operating in multiple international markets. He has argued this plays into HSBC's strengths - global scale and networks unmatched by local players.
Hughes has been readying his troops, recently hiring Swami Nagarajan as head of securities services in Australia and New Zealand and ex-Deutsche Bank operator Preethi Visweswara as head of structured finance.
